description:
Requests are failing across an entire region.

Analyst answer: It is our cloud object store, and products relying on it are having trouble too. We were looking into unusually slow billing progress. An engineer followed our usual operating procedure to take a handful of machines out of infrastructure supporting that process. Failures appeared abruptly this morning in our US East location, affecting users of the object store and products relying on it. We cannot read, enumerate, write or erase objects through the APIs. Virtual machine provisioning, disk volumes that fetch snapshot contents from the object store, on-demand function execution and the storage control panel are having trouble. Our status page controls will not let us post product-specific notices either.

triage.trigger: An engineer followed our usual operating procedure to take a handful of machines out of infrastructure supporting the billing process
symptoms: cannot read, enumerate, write or erase objects through APIs
disk volumes fetching snapshot contents failing
status page controls cannot post product-specific notices

real_root_cause: An authorized team member entered an incorrect input when executing a standard operational command intended to remove a small number of servers from a subsystem used by the object storage billing process. The incorrect input caused a much larger set of servers to be removed than intended, including servers supporting the metadata index and storage placement subsystems. The index subsystem manages object metadata and location information and is required for GET, LIST, PUT, and DELETE requests. The placement subsystem allocates storage for new objects during PUT requests and depends on the index subsystem. The loss of significant capacity forced both subsystems to undergo full restarts. Because of the service's growth, restarting the subsystems and performing metadata integrity checks took longer than expected.

description:
People are reporting failed connections.

Analyst answer: We run a live messaging application. Certain chat communities look disconnected, their hosting workers are acting strangely, and people are struggling to join. Early this afternoon our hosting vendor automatically relocated the machine serving as our active Redis server. It went out of reach and its standby assumed the active role. The first alert came early in the afternoon, and API behavior normalized roughly an hour afterward. About three quarters of an hour later, our dashboards flagged fresh trouble and community access complaints arrived almost immediately; only some communities appear affected, and we cannot quantify the user impact. Several API workers initially struggled to connect to Redis, calls were slow, and clients were hammering a costly API operation. Now certain chat communities look disconnected, one hosting worker is unhealthy, and several workers maintaining client sessions are acting strangely.

triage.trigger: our hosting vendor automatically relocated the machine serving as our active Redis server
symptoms: API workers unable to connect to Redis
workers maintaining client sessions acting strangely

real_root_cause: The initial disruption began when an automatic cloud infrastructure migration caused the primary node of a highly available Redis cluster to become unavailable. Although the cluster correctly failed over to its secondary, a previously known bug in how API instances handled Redis failover caused significant API degradation. This disruption also exposed an incorrectly configured edge caching rule for an expensive API endpoint, leading clients to make excessive requests and overloading a non-critical Cassandra cluster. The initial disruption was followed by failures in the real-time infrastructure: nodes in other services entered abnormal states, eventually ran out of memory, and contributed to a cascading system failure. The exact mechanism connecting the initial API disruption to the wider cascading failure was not determined. A later investigation identified potential flaws in a library used by an affected service, but their precise role in the cascade remained uncertain.

description:
Updates are taking much longer than usual.

Analyst answer: The shared cluster that lets our applications locate one another is in poor health. Credential delivery is sluggish too, and numerous backend applications rely on that infrastructure. During the preceding afternoon we switched a request-routing application to continuous updates from the coordination system and grew its fleet by roughly half. Operations seemed fine for close to a day, so the connection remains uncertain. Internal trouble surfaced in the early afternoon without affecting players initially. Several hours later we had roughly half our usual concurrent players, and conditions are still worsening.

triage.trigger: we switched a request-routing application to continuous updates from the coordination system and grew its fleet by roughly half
symptoms: updates are taking much longer than usual
shared service-discovery cluster is in poor health

real_root_cause: The outage resulted from two primarily independent performance problems within Consul. First, the recently enabled streaming implementation suffered excessive contention under the combination of very high read and write loads. The streaming implementation used fewer Go channels for concurrency control than the previous long-polling approach. At this workload scale, contention on a shared channel blocked writes, increased CPU usage, and severely degraded Consul performance. The 128-core replacement servers, which used a dual-socket NUMA architecture, aggravated contention on shared resources. Second, the workload exposed a pathological BoltDB performance problem affecting Consul's Raft log persistence. BoltDB retained free pages from deleted log entries in an increasingly large freelist. The database contained approximately 3.8 GB of unused space and a 7.8 MB freelist, which was rewritten during small log appends, causing excessive write latency. Backpressure and full TCP buffers contributed to write times of 2 to 3 seconds on unhealthy leaders. Both problems affected a single shared Consul cluster that supported numerous critical services, amplifying the outage. Monitoring systems also depended on Consul, reducing visibility during diagnosis.

description:
People are locked out of their accounts.

Analyst answer: The browser side of our CI offering is unavailable, including job output and help pages. Jobs themselves keep running and review results are still posted. We cut hosting expenses by moving our hosted Postgres deployment onto a less powerful tier recently. Instead of maintaining a pool on each app machine, we now share one pooling host. Postgres began slowing in the late afternoon UTC, with the site becoming largely unreachable roughly an hour and a half afterward. Account access, job output and help pages are unavailable to everyone trying to reach them; we have no evidence of a regional boundary.

triage.trigger: We cut hosting expenses by moving our hosted Postgres deployment onto a less powerful tier recently. Instead of maintaining a pool on each app machine, we now share one pooling host.
symptoms: people are locked out of their accounts
CI browser side unavailable including job output and help pages

real_root_cause: The smaller managed PostgreSQL instance could not handle the production workload during peak traffic, causing CPU saturation and database performance degradation. The application's health-check endpoint depended on successful connections to both SQL databases, Redis, and Memcached. When database connections failed, the health checks returned HTTP 500 errors, causing the dashboard load balancer to remove its application servers. Auto Scaling Groups launched replacement servers, but the server bootstrap process attempted to retrieve the currently deployed code revision from an endpoint on the unavailable website. Because that endpoint could not be reached, replacement servers ran the older application version embedded in their machine images. That version's health check referenced a database that had already been decommissioned, so replacement servers also failed health checks and could not join the load balancer. The resulting repeated instance launches and terminations eventually exhausted cloud instance request limits. Recovery was further delayed by cloud provider access-management issues and an on-call alerting configuration that failed to wake the team. The centralized pgbouncer configuration was reverted during recovery, but the post-mortem did not establish it as a confirmed root cause.

description:
Availability has suddenly plummeted.

Analyst answer: The backend that supplies customer account information is struggling, and its role in access checks means that the management console and numerous API operations are failing too. We shipped a console update roughly an hour and a half earlier, followed by an account backend revision just minutes before the failures appeared. Things went downhill late in the UTC afternoon. People opening the console or updating settings programmatically are having trouble, whereas our production traffic handling still seems normal.

triage.trigger: we shipped a console update roughly an hour and a half earlier, followed by an account backend revision just minutes before the failures appeared

real_root_cause: A bug introduced in the React dashboard caused excessive, unnecessary requests to the tenant API service. A React useEffect hook included an object in its dependency array that was recreated whenever component state or props changed. React therefore treated the object as a new dependency and repeatedly executed the effect, causing multiple requests to the /organizations endpoint during a single dashboard render instead of one. This behavior, combined with a concurrent tenant service update and insufficient capacity to handle traffic spikes, overwhelmed the tenant service. Because the tenant service participated in API authorization, its failure prevented authorization evaluation and caused widespread HTTP 5xx responses. Service restarts also triggered a thundering-herd pattern, with dashboards attempting to re-authenticate simultaneously, further amplified by the request-loop bug. During recovery, a patch intended to eliminate remaining service errors worsened availability and caused a second period of API impact.

description:
We suddenly have a surge of authorization failures.

Analyst answer: The errors are coming from our worldwide key-based data store. Web publishing, identity checks and releases of edge workloads are among the products relying on it. We were introducing a fresh storage build in stages. As the rollout advanced, monitoring warned of requests heading toward an unintended target; we tried to revert and the disruption quickly widened. Routing warnings appeared in the evening UTC, roughly a quarter of an hour before the broader disruption. Several products used by customers are impaired, but workloads independent of this storage layer and certain established login sessions continue to function. Storage reads, writes, removals and key enumeration are rejected as unauthorized. Hosted static websites throw server-side errors, sign-in is unreliable, publishing edge programs fails and other dependent features are down. Identity failures are also keeping us from using our regular release reversal tools.

triage.trigger: we were introducing a fresh storage build in stages
symptoms: surge of authorization failures on worldwide key-based data store
storage reads writes removals and key enumeration rejected as unauthorized

real_root_cause: A latent bug in our progressive deployment tool caused its release-listing API to return builds from both staging and production instead of restricting results to the requested environment. During the production rollout, the deployment automation incorrectly selected a script deployed to the staging account rather than the intended production-account build. The production routing configuration consequently pointed to a version that was not running in the production environment and was not authorized for production access. Requests to the key-value store were effectively routed into a black hole and returned HTTP 401 errors, causing failures across dependent services. Recovery was further delayed because our dashboard and CI authentication mechanisms themselves depended on the unavailable key-value store, preventing the normal rollback process from accessing the necessary secrets.

description:
Groups of servers are dropping together.

Analyst answer: Our advertising gateway is down: it accepts requests, handles competitive bidding and delivers the selected creative. All traffic entering our advertising platform goes through it. We had started pushing a change from our internal data store to machines around the globe after it cleared the live-environment checks. We do not yet know whether that change explains the failures. It came on abruptly in the early evening UTC. Nearly a thousand instances at roughly half a dozen sites went down together; neither direct deals nor outside exchanges are getting ads delivered anywhere.

triage.trigger: we had started pushing a change from our internal data store to machines around the globe after it cleared the live-environment checks

real_root_cause: An old double-free bug in the ad auction and serving service was triggered by an internal database update that deleted a rarely changed in-memory object. The service used time-based memory reclamation, which deferred freeing the object's memory until a later time. A defect caused the object to be deleted twice, resulting in a crash when the deferred deletion executed. The production validation systems initially accepted the update because the deletion had been scheduled but had not yet executed. The validation process did not wait for the deferred deletion window to pass before authorizing distribution, so the faulty update reached the production servers worldwide before the delayed crashes became visible. Test coverage for this rarely changed portion of the data model was also incomplete.

description:
People can't open their code projects.

Analyst answer: It's our online workspace for software teams, running on Postgres with a main instance paired with a live replica. Synchronization had failed, so we were reconstructing the replica by hand. We tried taking a fresh physical copy and adjusted the limits for replication streams and client sessions. Database demand spiked in the evening; synchronization trouble emerged roughly four hours afterward, with widespread downtime about half an hour later. Our shared hosted offering is affected, whereas independent installations and dedicated customer deployments are working.

triage.trigger: Database demand spiked in the evening; we were reconstructing the Postgres replica by hand, took a fresh physical copy, and adjusted limits for replication streams and client sessions
symptoms: users cannot open their code projects

real_root_cause: During manual recovery of the PostgreSQL standby, an engineer accidentally executed a data-directory removal operation on the primary database server instead of the secondary. The operation was stopped within seconds, but approximately 300 GB of production database data had already been removed. The repair work had been necessary because increased database load caused replication lag, and WAL segments required by the standby had already been removed from the primary without WAL archiving. The increased load involved both spam activity and a background process attempting to remove an employee account and its associated data after an erroneous abuse report. Recovery was severely complicated by unavailable backups: the logical backup job was using pg_dump 9.2 against PostgreSQL 9.6, causing the backups to fail. Failure notifications were rejected because the automated emails lacked the required DMARC configuration, leaving the team unaware of the problem. Database disk snapshots were not enabled, and the secondary had already been cleared during the replication repair. As a result, the team had to recover from an older LVM snapshot in staging, losing subsequent database modifications.

description:
Users say the page will not load.

Analyst answer: Our automated software integration system is affected. People cannot open the dashboard or launch build jobs. We still have no confirmed trigger. The failures surfaced as we were finishing a separate outage, and we are reviewing recent releases and infrastructure modifications. Trouble began shortly after midnight UTC. Our telemetry flagged poor performance roughly ten minutes later and kept showing it for about half an hour. Users cannot reach the dashboard or launch builds; several services are involved, but we have no reliable breakdown by region or affected user share.
real_root_cause: An operator inadvertently modified a Web Application Firewall (WAF) rule while investigating routine security monitoring, believing the actions were read-only. A misconfiguration in IAM permissions allowed the operator's role to modify infrastructure directly, bypassing the standard Terraform deployment process. The modified rule blocked legitimate traffic to two CDN distributions serving the platform's web interface and API. Because the change occurred outside Terraform, investigators initially had no corresponding deployment record and did not prioritize investigating the WAF configuration. Automated Terraform drift detection eventually identified the unauthorized configuration difference approximately 80 minutes after the initial change.

description:
Our automated checks are failing sporadically.

Analyst answer: We monitor a hosted database offering, and the failing step is the probe that provisions a new container. Our provisioning logic and request method have been unchanged for months. We are unaware of anything changing just before the errors appeared. We noticed the first rejection in the early evening UTC and marked availability as degraded roughly half an hour afterward. US East was hit first, with roughly three quarters of probes unsuccessful; locations elsewhere remained healthy. Requests to provision containers keep getting rejected because a parameter is deemed unacceptable. Some attempts pass, and the diagnostics do not tell us which parameter caused the rejection.

symptoms: container provisioning requests rejected because a parameter is deemed unacceptable

real_root_cause: The cloud database provider introduced an unannounced breaking change to its API contract. A partition key field that had previously been optional became mandatory when creating database containers. Our existing SDK-based implementation did not explicitly supply this field, causing container creation requests to fail as the change progressively affected different regions.
